questions.author: owner
questions.question: What led the owner to go in with real capital, and was that backed by tests in any way?
questions.reference: Partly. A staged entry was first recommended on 19.08 from 365-day walk-forwards over 22 windows, in which two Base pools passed the gate (cbBTC/WETH 0.05% at 82% winning windows and worst -1.8, WETH/USDC 0.05% at 68% and -2.6); paper trading was then only two days old and left out of the weights. On 26.08 the 720-day window failed every configuration and the money waited in USDC. On 27.08, before entering, the owner had two more tests run: a 90-day replay with $2.5k per pool, where a fresh window (29.05 to 27.08, ETH +24.7%) reversed the stale window's verdict while the ranking stayed the same in both (passive wide >= HODL >= flat-only >= active), and his own FlatWide hybrid, implemented and computed before entry on 365 days for both pools, which came out at least as good as pure passive wide on both. He chose the hybrid on both pools and entered the same day through the cockpit; the journal records the entry as an operational experiment on a small stake, with a FOMO note.

facts.a: 19.08 recommendation of a staged entry rested on 365-day walk-forwards (22 windows): two Base pools passed the gate (cbBTC/WETH 82% / -1.8, WETH/USDC 0.05% 68% / -2.6)
facts.b: paper trading was then only two days old and left out of the weights
facts.c: the owner's FlatWide hybrid was tested before entry on 365 days for both pools: at least as good as pure passive wide on both

questions.author: owner
questions.question: How was a position rebalanced, that is, how were the ranges moved: was it the same position or did a new one have to be opened, and did it happen automatically or did a new transaction have to be made?
questions.reference: A range cannot be moved on an existing Uniswap v3 position, so a rebalance closed the old position and opened a new one, and nothing happened automatically: approving a rebalance proposal meant two or three signatures in Rabby, in order. Step 1 is one multicall on the NFT position manager, decreaseLiquidity of 100% plus collect, so fees come out with the liquidity; step 2 is a swap that evens out the token proportions for the new range (exactInputSingle on SwapRouter02 in the same pool), skipped when the deviation is under 2% of the value; step 3 is the mint of the new range, rebuilt just before sending from the actual balances (the plan only holds an estimate), with an extra approval if the real amount exceeds the approved one. Progress is saved in the browser (localStorage), so a failure in the middle leaves the funds safe in the wallet and the window offers to finish the remaining step (for example 'finish step 2/3').

facts.a: not automatic: approving a rebalance proposal meant two or three signatures in Rabby, in order
facts.b: step 1: one multicall on the NFT position manager, decreaseLiquidity 100% + collect
facts.c: step 2: a swap evening out the token proportions in the same pool, skipped when the deviation is under 2% of value
facts.d: step 3: mint of the new range, rebuilt from the actual balances just before sending (extra approve if needed)
facts.e: progress saved in localStorage: a failure mid-way leaves the funds in the wallet and the UI offers 'finish step 2/3'

spans.reason: section 6, rebalance sequence: two or three Rabby signatures, multicall decrease+collect, proportion swap skipped when close, mint, safe state and 'finish step 2/3'

questions.author: CC-Mac
questions.question: Why did HOMOS stick to major tokens instead of the exotic pools that advertised much higher yields?
questions.reference: Because the advertised yields did not survive a test with real swaps. The pool-selection meta-backtest of 10.08 showed exotic pools at 74.8% fee-APR against 50.7% for majors, but without impermanent loss. A tick-level backtest of WTAO/WETH 1% on mainnet (90 days, 10 750 swaps) then showed a real fee yield of about 5-20% a year for a passive position, the pool's result dominated by the token's own price, and narrow ranges on a trending exotic realising losses (±5%: $1 316 of fees but -33.8 points vs HODL). On 10.08 the exotic sleeve was set to 0% and the majors-only filter counted as confirmed by a third independent test; exposure to an exotic was a bet on the token, not an LP strategy. On 11.08 that table turned out to be in the wrong units (WTAO treated as a $1 stable, so the 'uptrend' was a fall, HODL -70.5% a year); the reasoning was corrected (the token's beta of -70% a year crushes an LP alpha of about +7 points) and majors-only stayed.

facts.a: 10.08 meta-backtest: exotics 74.8% vs majors 50.7% fee-APR, but without impermanent loss
facts.b: tick-level WTAO/WETH 1% (90 days, 10 750 swaps): real passive fee yield ~5-20%/yr, result dominated by the token's beta; narrow ranges realise losses
facts.c: 10.08: exotic sleeve 0%, majors-only confirmed by a third independent test; an exotic is a bet on the token, not an LP strategy
facts.d: 11.08 correction: the table was in WTAO units (a fall, not a rise); token beta -70%/yr crushes LP alpha ~+7 pp; majors-only stays

spans.reason: key caveat: exotics 74.8% vs majors-only 50.7% fee-APR, without IL

questions.author: CC-Mac
questions.question: How were the rebalance swaps protected against MEV sandwich attacks?
questions.reference: The corpus has the requirement but no implementation. The 10.08 plan says a rebalance includes a swap, so a bot sending transactions through the public mempool would be sandwiched regularly, and it requires a private RPC or protected transactions, slippage limits computed from the current pool depth and deadlines, adding that the problem is smaller on an L2 than on mainnet but not zero. Nothing records a private RPC or protected transactions being set up. The only protection recorded is the slippage limit: the proportion swap of a rebalance carries a minimum output (in the 10.08 builder test, spot minus the 0.3% pool fee minus 0.5% slippage), and the live capital was on Base, an L2.

related.reason: section 3.5 MEV and execution: sandwiching through the public mempool, private RPC / protected transactions, slippage from depth, deadlines, smaller on L2
10.08 builder test: swap with min out = spot minus 0.3% fee minus 0.5% slippage

questions.author: CC-Mac
questions.question: Which machine-learning model did the bot use to predict where the price would go?
questions.reference: None was used or built. The only mention of machine learning in the corpus is a literature finding from the 26.08 review: ML and reinforcement learning give results on the scale of the project's own experiments, not a breakthrough. The project's question was whether a rules-based strategy with no discretion and no forecasting could beat holding the same two tokens, and the bot's choices came from fixed rules calibrated in backtests (pool ranking by 7-day fee yield, range width w = k x sigma x sqrt(7d) from measured volatility). The only 'forecast' in the application was a profit-forecast panel showing backtest APRs of the hard-coded v1.2 strategies from a file of 17.08; it was removed on 29.08 because it showed an algorithm that was no longer played.
